summary: Titanium is a Java dialect for scientific computing with a partitioned global address space, SPMD parallelism, and multi-dimensional domain-based arrays. The paper reviews its design, compiler analyses and runtime, and reports results on NAS FT and MG and on AMR and immersed boundary applications.
why_read: It is a long-form account of how a PGAS language was designed, compiled and used on real applications, with the reasoning behind each choice.
main_contribution: A PGAS Java dialect with domain calculus, textually aligned barriers, and a C-emitting compiler with concurrency, alias and locality analyses over GASNet.
main_limitation: The authors leave distributed garbage collection and region safety unresolved, and their expressiveness evidence is line counts rather than a controlled study.
evaluation_method: Measured speedups and runtimes on six production clusters against Fortran with MPI and Chombo, plus line counts and GASNet microbenchmarks.
notes: Catalog id has year 1998, but the supplied PDF is the 2007 IJHPCA article (Vol. 21, No. 3, pp. 266-290, DOI 10.1177/1094342007078449) with first author K. Yelick. The 1998 Titanium paper (Yelick et al. 1998, Concurrency: Practice and Experience 10:825-836) is cited in its introduction and reference list, so the id may refer to that earlier work. The card describes the PDF supplied. The title matches the PDF metadata.
